title: When the Guard Adds Nothing: A Preregistered Paired Evaluation of Generate–Validate–Repair for LLM‑Produced Vendor CLI Configurations
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment (n=300 task pairs) that measured whether a deterministic generate–validate–repair (G‑V‑R) pipeline increases the probability that an LLM‑produced vendor CLI configuration passes a conservative deterministic validator, compared to direct LLM generation. The preregistration froze a shared initial candidate per task (one generator call shared by both arms) and a bounded guarded policy that allows at most one automatic repair call if the shared initial failed. Under the declared prompt and generator snapshot (gpt‑5‑mini) every shared initial candidate passed the deterministic validator (baseline = 300/300; guarded = 300/300). The preregistered paired test yields n11 = 300, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0; paired difference = 0.00; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10k resamples, seed = 1729). Because no initial failures occurred, the preregistered single‑repair policy was not invoked. All execution artifacts (task manifest, model configuration, raw responses, provider traces, validator traces, analysis inputs/outputs) are archived and hash‑signed to enable exact reproduction.

sections.introduction: Generative LLMs are increasingly proposed to translate operator intent into vendor CLI changes for NetOps automation. A practical reliability architecture for such pipelines is generate–validate–repair (G‑V‑R): a generator proposes a candidate configuration, a deterministic validator enforces syntactic and workflow invariants, and a repair module attempts bounded corrections when the validator fails. This study asks a tightly scoped confirmatory question: under a shared‑initial paired design (the same initial generator output is used for both arms), does a single automatic repair attempt (guarded arm) increase the probability of producing a validator‑passing configuration compared to direct generation without repair (baseline arm)? We preregistered the design, executed the run end‑to‑end, and archive every artifact (preregistration, task manifest, model configuration, provider traces, validator traces, and analysis outputs) so all numerical claims below are directly traceable to hashed artifacts.
sections.related_work: Prior work on intent‑to‑configuration and LLM‑assisted NetOps includes intent‑based translation frameworks and recent LLM‑for‑NetOps proposals (see representative verification and intent papers cited in the artifact bundle). Deterministic verification and SMT‑based configuration verification (Bagpipe/Weitz et al., 2016) motivate our conservative validator design. Tool‑assisted self‑refinement and bounded repair literature motivate a limited repair budget rather than unconstrained iterative correction. We restricted citations to verified primary sources and include artifact pointers in the reproducibility section so readers can reconcile our positioning with the underlying archives.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and estimand. We preregistered a paired binary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (study_hosted_netops_gvr_v1_cnd_7a3f2b1e; preregistration SHA‑256 = a85d66d4c6ce2275e2d8c820f96c610532dbb5452bebb3fe108848f9dc38cdf6). Design. For each of 300 tasks the pipeline produced one shared initial candidate (one model call). Baseline outcome: validator(initial). Guarded outcome: validator(initial); if initial failed, a single automatic repair call was allowed and the repaired candidate revalidated. This enforces a paired, shared‑initial comparison where any observed advantage can be attributed to the single repair step. Tasks and validator. The curated 300‑task multi‑vendor manifest (execution/task_manifest.jsonl; SHA‑256 = 6d99060659a722e6a91dd2abd7baca45a2aefb41e124b049124d5ea2632cb4b3) contains explicit safe‑sequence constraints, required final states, and vendor labels. Validator. deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (version 5.0) enforces parsing/canonicalization, syntactic correctness, interface assignment invariants, workflow ordering constraints (e.g., make‑before‑break, down‑before‑change when required), and destructive‑pattern detection. Execution contract and model snapshot. The declared model snapshot was gpt‑5‑mini (execution/model_configuration.json; SHA‑256 = 1acce92558edeb13cd97b75817329d332afe4a36d01d566f1a26c61b132923fa). The adapter family was hosted_netops_gvr_v1 in scientific_confirmatory mode with planned episodes = 600 (two arms × 300 tasks) and a preregistered maximum of one repair call per guarded episode. Analysis plan. Primary test: exact McNemar two‑sided test on paired binary outcomes; paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI with 10,000 resamples (seed = 1729) as pre‑specified. Secondary analyses included per‑vendor paired comparisons with Bonferroni correction; those were pre‑specified and executed as described below. Reproducibility. All raw responses, provider traces, validator traces, and analysis inputs/outputs are archived with SHA‑256 hashes (execution manifest and analysis artifacts paths and hashes are supplied in the artifact bundle).
sections.results: Execution bookkeeping. The run completed exactly as preregistered: planned episodes = 600; completed episodes = 600; failed episodes = 0. Provider calls: 300 completed hosted model call events (one shared initial generation per task); model_calls_used = 300; cache hits = 0 (full provider trace directory archived under execution/provider_calls/; representative file execution/provider_calls/task-000001-shared-initial.json, SHA‑256 = a59191a39575bd602217f53eac4f3e5c6ef03b203d3dd678edcb06f8964e5e49). Confirmatory numeric outcome. The deterministic scoring artifacts show that every shared initial candidate passed the validator without repairs: baseline_success_count = 300/300 and guarded_success_count = 300/300. The paired contingency table (guarded × baseline) is n11 = 300, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv; SHA‑256 = a39fd3386c945cae095f2f310ead1f21ac600f8b2492bcd49b664c8da5782aa0). The exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00. The paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10k resamples, seed = 1729) is [0.00, 0.00]; the estimate of the paired difference is 0.00. Repair invocation. Because there were zero initial validator failures across all tasks, the preregistered single‑repair policy was never invoked (repair call count = 0); this is recorded in the per‑episode validator traces (examples: execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json SHA‑256 = 1c3cbbeb30cb9d0...). Representative episodes. Example archived episodes (shared initial, baseline, guarded) and validator diagnostics are provided in the execution scoring directory (see above example artifact paths and SHA values).
sections.discussion: Statistical and operational interpretation. The paired shared‑initial design isolates the marginal contribution of a single repair attempt applied only when the identical initial candidate failed. In this run the generator + prompt + model snapshot produced a ceiling outcome: every shared initial candidate satisfied the conservative deterministic validator, so there were no discordant pairs for the repair stage to change. The observed paired difference is exactly 0.00 with McNemar p = 1.00 and the bootstrap CI collapsed to the degenerate point [0.00, 0.00] because discordance is zero. This is an artifact‑grounded factual outcome recorded in analysis/analysis_log.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 7bc0bb7defe3ae318bf05df517894823264f574116027384f3627e4517e9713b). Review request on per‑vendor secondary tests. The preregistration included per‑vendor paired comparisons; those secondary tests were executed exactly as specified. Because there were no discordant pairs overall, the per‑vendor subgroup paired tests were likewise uninformative (no discordant pairs observed within any vendor subgroup). We therefore report that the preregistered per‑vendor paired comparisons produced no discordant pairs and hence no additional inference—this conclusion is directly verifiable from the canonical manifest and scoring artifacts (execution/task_manifest.jsonl; SHA‑256 = 6d99060659a722e6a91dd2abd7baca45a2aefb41e124b049124d5ea2632cb4b3 and analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv; SHA‑256 = a39fd3386c945cae095f2f310ead1f21ac600f8b2492bcd49b664c8da5782aa0). External validity and the shared‑initial tradeoff. The shared‑initial design intentionally reduces generator variance to attribute any improvement to the repair stage, but this comes at a cost: when the generator is already accurate on the selected task distribution, the design produces ceiling effects that eliminate observable repair benefit. This tradeoff is a construct‑validity consideration: the estimator answers a specific causal question (value of repair conditional on the same initial candidate) but reduces sensitivity to cases where the generator would produce differing initial candidates across arms. Suggested follow‑ups that the archived artifacts enable (no new evidence claimed here): (1) remove the shared‑initial constraint and draw independent initial candidates per arm to measure repair impact under generator variability; (2) expand or adversarially harden the task manifest to increase initial failure incidence; (3) permit iterative repair or human‑in‑the‑loop interventions; (4) evaluate other model snapshots and prompt templates. All follow‑ups are directly reproducible from the archived manifest and scripts.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment that isolated the marginal effect of a bounded single automatic repair on a shared LLM candidate across 300 multi‑vendor NetOps intents. For the declared prompt and gpt‑5‑mini snapshot every shared initial candidate passed a conservative deterministic validator, so the preregistered single‑repair policy was never invoked and produced no measurable benefit (paired difference = 0.00; exact McNemar p = 1.00; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00]). The empirical result is narrow and artifact‑anchored: when the declared generator configuration already produces validator‑passing outputs on the chosen task distribution, adding a bounded repair stage does not increase deterministic pass rates but does add cost. All artifacts (preregistration, task manifest, model configuration, raw responses, provider traces, validator traces, and analysis outputs) are archived and hash‑signed to support exact reproduction and controlled follow‑ups that vary prompt, model snapshot, task hardness, or repair budget.

limitations: Single model snapshot (gpt-5-mini) evaluated — results do not generalize to other models or model versions.

Deterministic validator implements a conservative subset of operational hazards (syntactic checks, interface and workflow invariants) and omits dynamic/emulation‑level checks and deeper routing semantics.

Curated 300‑task manifest may not include adversarial or out‑of‑distribution failure modes; under the chosen prompt and model snapshot every shared initial candidate passed the validator (ceiling effect), limiting the ability to measure G‑V‑R improvements under the preregistered one‑repair policy.

Shared initial‑candidate design (preregistered) fixes the same initial generation for both arms to isolate repair effect; this reduces sensitivity to generator variability and can mask repair value when the generator is already accurate on the task set.
Only a single automatic repair attempt was permitted per task; iterative or human‑in‑the‑loop repair policies were not evaluated.
Automated contamination detection cannot eliminate memorization risk entirely; the preregistered contamination summary reported zero flagged pairs but residual uncertainty remains.
